105865.q: What are the bald areas at the temples called, which often appear first when someone starts going bald?
105865.e: In inherited hair loss, the hairline often moves back at the temples first. This is called a receding hairline.
105865.m: A receding hairline means the hair moves back at the temples.

105866.q: What is a bald spot on the top of the back of the head called, which recalls a hairstyle monks used to wear?
105866.e: Monks used to have a round patch on the back of the head shaved bald, called the tonsure. The bald patch that forms on top of the head in many men looks similar.
105866.m: The tonsure is a bald patch on the top of the head.

105867.q: What mainly decides whether a man goes bald?
105867.e: The most common baldness comes from inherited hair loss: from birth, the hair roots are sensitive to certain hormones made by the body. Hats or washing play no part in it.

105868.q: Why is the skin of a bald head especially at risk in summer?
a: It has no sun protection from hair
It is thicker than other skin
It has a poorer blood supply
105868.e: Hair shades the scalp. Without it, UV rays hit the skin directly, which is why a hat or sun cream is important.
105868.m: A bald head needs a hat or sun cream in summer.

105869.q: What is usually moved in a hair transplant?
a: The person’s own hair roots from the back of the head
105869.e: In a hair transplant, the person’s own hair follicles are taken from the back of the head and put into bald areas. There they keep growing.
105869.m: In a hair transplant, your own hair moves to a new place.

105870.q: Why does a ring of hair often remain at the back and sides of many bald heads?
a: The hair roots there are less sensitive by inheritance
You lie on it at night
105870.e: The hair roots at the back and sides of the head do not react to the hormones involved in inherited hair loss. That is why a ring of hair often remains there.
105870.m: The ring of hair stays because its roots are tougher.

105871.q: Roughly what share of men have visible inherited hair loss by the age of 50?
105871.e: Inherited hair loss is very common. By about 50, around half of all men are affected to a greater or lesser degree.
105871.m: About one man in two has hair loss by 50.

105872.q: Where does the hair usually get thinner when women have inherited hair loss?
a: At the parting on top of the head
Only at the nape of the neck
105872.e: In women, the hair usually thins over a wide area around the parting. Going completely bald is rare for them.
105872.m: In women, the hair usually gets thinner at the parting.

105873.q: Why does hair turn grey with age?
a: The hair roots make less pigment
105873.e: In the hair roots, pigment cells make the pigment melanin. With age these cells work less, and colourless hairs grow.
105873.m: Grey hair appears when the hair roots make less pigment.

105874.q: Do more grey hairs grow back if you pull out a grey hair?
a: No, only one hair grows from each follicle
Yes, two or three grow back
Yes, all the neighbouring hairs turn grey
105874.e: A hair follicle only ever makes one hair, and pulling one out does not affect the neighbouring follicles. Getting more grey hair comes only from getting older.
105874.m: Pulling out grey hairs does not make more grey hairs grow.

105875.q: Why does a hair without pigment look white?
a: Tiny air bubbles scatter the light
105875.e: Colourless hair contains tiny pockets of air. They scatter the light in all directions, a bit like snow, which is why the hair looks white.
105875.m: Air in the hair makes colourless hairs look white.

105876.q: Can a dark hair that has already grown turn grey overnight?
a: No, only hair that grows back is colourless
105876.e: The hair shaft is dead, and its pigment stays. A hair only turns grey if it grows out of the root already colourless.
105876.m: A hair that has grown does not lose its colour overnight.

105877.q: If you look closely, what is “grey” hair usually?
a: A mixture of coloured and white hairs
Hair with grey dust on it
105877.e: A single hair is usually either still coloured or already white. Only the mixture of both looks grey from a distance.
105877.m: Hair looks grey because of the mix of coloured and white hairs.

105878.q: From what age do many people get their first grey hairs?
105878.e: Many people get their first grey hairs between about 30 and 40. Exactly when depends strongly on their genes.
105878.m: The first grey hairs often appear between 30 and 40.

105879.q: Why do grey roots show again a few weeks after grey hair has been dyed?
a: The hair growing back is still colourless
The dye moves into the scalp
The dye is destroyed by light
The hair rejects the dye straight away
105879.e: Hair dye only works on hair that has already grown. Colourless hair keeps growing out of the root, and it can be seen at the scalp as roots.
105879.m: Dyed hair grows back in its natural colour at the root.

105880.q: What is the pigment called that gives hair and skin their colour?
105880.e: Melanin is made in special cells of the skin and hair roots. Depending on its type and amount, hair is blond, brown, black or red.

105881.q: Roughly what share of the hairs on the head are in the growth phase at the same time?
105881.e: Every hair has its own rhythm. The vast majority are growing, and only a small number are resting or about to fall out, which is why all your hair never falls out at once.
105881.m: Most hairs on the head are growing at the same time, only a few are resting.

105883.q: Roughly how long does the growth phase of a hair on the head last?
105883.e: A hair on the head usually grows for between 2 and 6 years without a break. Then it moves into the transition and resting phases.
105883.m: A hair on the head grows for several years.

105884.q: A hair grows 1 cm per month. How long is it after 3 years of non-stop growth?
105884.e: 3 years are 3 times 12, so 36 months. At 1 cm per month, the hair grows 36 times 1 cm, so 36 cm.
105884.m: To work out hair length, multiply the growth per month by the number of months.

105885.q: Why do eyelashes and eyebrows stay much shorter than the hair on your head?
a: Their growth phase is much shorter
They are not made of keratin
105885.e: Eyelashes and eyebrows only grow for a few months, then they fall out and are replaced. Hair on the head, by contrast, keeps growing for years.
105885.m: The short growth phase keeps eyelashes and eyebrows short.

105886.q: Lena’s hair is 20 cm long and grows 1.2 cm per month. How long is it after 10 months without a haircut?
105886.e: In 10 months the hair grows 10 times 1.2 cm, so 12 cm. 20 cm plus 12 cm makes 32 cm.
105886.m: Add the growth of all the months to the starting length.

105887.q: A person has 100,000 hairs on their head, and each grows 0.3 mm per day. How many metres of hair grow altogether per day?
105887.e: 100,000 times 0.3 mm makes 30,000 mm. Since 1000 mm make one metre, that is 30 m.
105887.m: Lots of small lengths add up to a long distance.

105888.q: A hair stops growing and rests for a while. What usually happens next?
a: It falls out and a new hair grows
It keeps growing twice as fast
It turns into a sweat gland
It stays on the head for ever
105888.e: Every hair goes through growth, a short transition and a resting time. Then it falls out, and a new hair grows from the same hair follicle.
105888.m: After its resting time, a hair falls out and is replaced.

105889.q: What is the skin under the nail called, on which the nail plate rests?
105889.e: The nail plate lies firmly on the nail bed and slowly slides forwards over it as it grows.
105889.m: The nail lies on the nail bed.

105890.q: Why does a healthy fingernail look pink?
a: Blood vessels in the nail bed show through
The nail plate is coloured pink
Light is bent red in the nail
105890.e: The nail plate is almost see-through. Below it lies the nail bed, which has a good blood supply, and its colour shows through.
105890.m: The pink of nails comes from the blood in the nail bed.

105891.q: In which area is the nail plate made?
a: In the nail matrix at the base of the nail
At the tip of the nail
At the side edge of the nail
105891.e: The nail matrix lies under the skin at the base of the nail. Its cells harden and push the nail plate forwards.
105891.m: The nail grows from the nail matrix at the base of the nail.

105892.q: What colour do nails often turn when the blood carries too little oxygen, for example in severe cold?
105892.e: Blood low in oxygen is darker. The nail bed then looks bluish through the see-through nail plate.
105892.m: Bluish nails show there is little oxygen in the blood.

105893.q: What job does the cuticle at the base of the nail have?
a: It protects the nail matrix from germs
It makes the nail grow faster
105893.e: The cuticle seals the gap between the skin and the nail. This means fewer germs reach the sensitive nail matrix.
105893.m: The cuticle seals the base of the nail against germs.

105894.q: How do toenails grow compared with fingernails?
105894.e: Toenails only grow about half as fast as fingernails. That is why a whole toenail takes around one to one and a half years to grow back.
105894.m: Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails.

105895.q: Roughly how long does it take for a whole fingernail to grow back?
105895.e: The nail slowly grows forwards from the nail matrix to the tip. It takes about half a year until it is completely renewed.
105895.m: A fingernail renews itself in about half a year.

105896.q: What forms when you trap your finger hard and blood flows under the nail?
a: A dark bruise under the nail
105896.e: The blow tears tiny vessels in the nail bed. The blood collects under the nail plate and shows through dark red to black.
105896.m: Trapping your finger can cause a bruise under the nail.

105897.q: What makes an ingrown toenail more likely?
a: Cutting the nail round instead of straight
105897.e: If the corners are cut round, the nail can grow sideways into the skin and make it inflamed. That is why toenails are cut straight.
105897.m: Cut toenails straight so they do not grow in.

105898.q: Which germs usually cause nail fungus?
105898.e: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi that feed on keratin. Less often, yeasts or moulds are involved.
105898.m: Nail fungus is usually caused by thread fungi.

105899.q: Where do people especially often catch nail or foot fungus?
a: Barefoot at indoor pools, saunas and showers
105899.e: Fungal spores survive well on damp floors. If you walk barefoot there, you can easily pick them up; pool sliders protect you.
105899.m: Pool sliders protect against fungi at pools and in showers.

105900.q: What kind of surroundings do nail fungi especially like?
105900.e: Fungi grow best in damp warmth, for example in tight, sweaty shoes. Airy shoes and dry feet make life hard for them.

105901.q: How can you often recognise nail fungus?
a: The nail becomes yellowish, thick and brittle
The nail becomes shiny and pink
The nail grows twice as fast
The nail becomes see-through and soft
105901.e: With nail fungus, the nail usually turns whitish to yellowish brown. It becomes thicker and crumbly and can come away from the nail bed.
105901.m: A yellow, thick and brittle nail can be a sign of nail fungus.

105902.q: Why does treating nail fungus often take many months?
a: The healthy nail has to grow back slowly
The medicines only work after years
The fungus hides in the bone
105902.e: The infected nail does not become healthy again; it has to be replaced by healthy nail growing back. Because nails grow slowly, this takes time.
105902.m: Nail fungus is only cured when a healthy nail has grown back.

105903.q: Which skin condition often comes before nail fungus on the toes?
105903.e: Athlete’s foot between the toes is very common. If it is not treated, the fungi can spread to the toenails.
105903.m: Untreated athlete’s foot can spread to the nails.

105904.q: How can you catch nail fungus from other people?
a: By shaking hands on the phone
105904.e: Fungal spores cling to towels, socks and shoes. That is why you should not share these things with others.
105904.m: Your own towels and shoes protect you from nail fungus.

105905.q: Are fingernails or toenails more often affected by nail fungus?
105905.e: Toenails often spend a long time in warm, damp shoes and grow slowly. That is why they are infected much more often than fingernails.
105905.m: Nail fungus mainly affects the toenails.

105906.q: What helps in everyday life to prevent nail fungus?
a: Drying your feet and the gaps between your toes well
Letting your nails grow as long as possible
105906.e: Dry skin between the toes gives fungi little to hold on to. Fresh socks every day and airy shoes also help.

105907.q: What can trigger a new flare-up of psoriasis?
105907.e: Psoriasis often comes in flare-ups. Infections, stress or certain medicines can trigger a new flare-up.
105907.m: Stress and infections can make psoriasis worse.

a: Yes, through shared plates and cups
105908.e: Psoriasis develops within the body itself, triggered by the immune system and an inherited tendency. You cannot catch it from people who have it.

105909.q: On which parts of the body does psoriasis appear especially often?
a: Earlobes and tips of the toes
105909.e: Typical patches appear on the outer sides of the elbows and knees and on the scalp. But other areas can be affected too.
105909.m: Psoriasis often appears on the elbows, knees and scalp.

105910.q: What happens differently in the skin with psoriasis?
a: The epidermis renews itself far too quickly
The skin makes no more cells
The skin loses all its hair
The skin is broken down by fungi
105910.e: Normally the epidermis renews itself in around four weeks. With psoriasis this happens in a few days, so the cells pile up and form scales.
105910.m: With psoriasis, the epidermis grows back far too quickly.

105911.q: What do typical patches of psoriasis look like?
105911.e: The patches have sharp edges, are red and slightly raised. On top lie shiny, silvery scales.
105911.m: Silvery scales on red skin are typical of psoriasis.

105912.q: How do the fingernails often change with psoriasis?
a: They all fall off at once
105912.e: Many people with it have pitted nails with small dents in the nail plate. Yellowish-brown patches, known as oil spots, also occur.
105912.m: Pits in the nails can be a sign of psoriasis.

105913.q: Which additional problem can some people with psoriasis have?
105913.e: In some people with psoriasis, the joints also become inflamed. This is called psoriatic arthritis.
105913.m: Psoriasis can also inflame the joints.

105914.q: Which treatment for psoriasis uses light in a targeted way?
105914.e: In light therapy, the skin is exposed to UV light in a controlled way. This slows down the excessive inflammation and the rapid cell division.
105914.m: Controlled UV light can ease psoriasis.

105915.q: What part does the immune system play in psoriasis?
a: It wrongly triggers inflammation in the skin
People with psoriasis have none at all
It only attacks fungi in the skin
It has nothing to do with it
105915.e: In psoriasis, the body’s defences overreact and cause inflammation in the skin. Flare-ups can be triggered by infections or stress, for example.
105915.m: Psoriasis is an inflammation that comes from the immune system.

a: A spot where the hair grows in a spiral
A bald spot on the head
105916.e: At a hair whorl, the hair follicles are angled so that the hairs grow in a circle around a central point.
105916.m: At a hair whorl, the hair grows in a circle.

105917.q: Where do most people have their hair whorl?
a: On the top of the head towards the back
In the middle of the forehead
At the nape of the neck
105917.e: The typical hair whorl is on the top of the back of the head. From there the hair spreads out in all directions.
105917.m: The hair whorl is usually on the top of the back of the head.

105918.q: In which direction does the hair whorl turn in most people?
105918.e: Studies show that in most people the whorl on the back of the head turns clockwise. In a minority it turns anticlockwise.

105919.q: What is it called when someone has two hair whorls on their head?
105919.e: Some people have two whorls next to each other on the back of the head. This is called a double crown; the hair there is often hard to style.
105919.m: Two hair whorls are called a double crown.

105920.q: Why is it hard to comb hair at a whorl in a different direction?
a: The direction of growth is fixed by the hair follicles
The hair there is electrically charged
105920.e: The hair follicles sit at an angle in the skin and set the direction of growth. Combing cannot change this for good.
105920.m: The angled follicles decide which way the hair grows.

105921.q: For which animal are hair whorls traditionally recorded in its passport for identification?
105921.e: In a horse passport, the position of the hair whorls is drawn in as well as the markings. They are different on every horse and do not change.
105921.m: Horses can also be recognised by their hair whorls.

105922.q: When is it decided where a person’s hair whorl will be?
105922.e: The hair follicles and their direction already form in the unborn child. That is why the hair whorl stays in the same place for life.
105922.m: The hair whorl forms before birth.

105923.q: How are head lice usually passed on?
a: By jumping from head to head
Through water in the swimming pool
105923.e: Head lice can neither jump nor fly. They mainly crawl onto another head when hair touches directly.
105923.m: Head lice move from head to head when hair touches.

105924.q: People with which natural hair colour usually have the most hairs on their head?
105924.e: Blond hairs are especially thin, but usually more of them grow, often around 150,000. Redheads have thicker hairs, but fewer of them.
105924.m: Blond people usually have the most but thinnest hairs on their head.

a: A shampoo with an anti-fungal ingredient
105925.e: Special anti-dandruff shampoos contain ingredients against the yeast fungus on the scalp. This calms the skin, and it makes fewer flakes.
105925.m: Anti-dandruff shampoos work against the fungus on the scalp.

105926.q: Which kind of living thing often encourages greasy dandruff?
105926.e: A yeast fungus that feeds on sebum lives on the scalp. If it multiplies a lot, it irritates the skin and more flakes form.
105926.m: A yeast fungus on the scalp can encourage dandruff.

105927.q: What is the line called where the scalp on the forehead meets skin without hair?
105927.e: The hairline is the line where the hair on the head begins. When hair loss starts, it can move backwards.
105927.m: Where the hair begins on the forehead is the hairline.

105928.q: What do head lice feed on?
105928.e: Head lice bite into the scalp several times a day and suck blood. Their saliva causes the typical itching.
105928.m: Head lice suck blood from the scalp.

105929.q: Why does a small cut on the scalp often bleed a lot?
a: The scalp has an especially good blood supply
The blood in the head is thinner
Blood does not clot on the head
105929.e: The scalp is supplied by many blood vessels that feed the hair roots. That is why even a small wound there bleeds heavily.
105929.m: The scalp has a rich blood supply and bleeds heavily when injured.

105930.q: What is the yellowish, scaly crust called that many babies have on their scalp in the first months of life?
105930.e: Cradle cap is a harmless, greasy flaking of the scalp in babies. It usually disappears by itself after a few months.
105930.m: Cradle cap is a harmless scaly crust in babies.

106224.q: What is the part of a tooth that sticks out of the gum and can be seen called?
106224.e: The crown is the part you see in your mouth and chew with. The root and the socket are hidden in the jawbone.
106224.m: The crown is the visible part of a tooth.

106225.q: Which layer covers the crown of a tooth on the outside?
106225.e: The crown is covered by a hard, shiny layer of enamel. It protects the more sensitive inside of the tooth.
106225.m: Enamel protects the crown like armour.

106226.q: What is the hardest substance in the human body?
106226.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals and is harder than any bone. That is why it stands up to chewing for decades.
106226.m: Tooth enamel is harder than any bone in the body.

106227.q: Which mineral is an important building block of tooth enamel?
106227.e: Tooth enamel is made almost entirely of minerals. The most important building block is calcium together with phosphate.
106227.m: Tooth enamel contains lots of calcium.

106228.q: Why can the body not rebuild lost tooth enamel itself?
a: Finished enamel contains no living cells
Enamel only grows back during sleep
Saliva dissolves new enamel straight away
Enamel only forms again during a fever
106228.e: The cells that build the enamel die as soon as the tooth has come through. That is why a hole in the enamel has to be filled by the dentist.
106228.m: Lost tooth enamel does not grow back.

106229.q: What are the fine grooves on the chewing surface of the back teeth, where decay easily starts, called?
106229.e: Fissures are narrow grooves between the bumps of the back teeth. Food scraps and bacteria easily get stuck there.
106229.m: Decay starts especially easily in the fissures of the back teeth.

106230.q: What are the raised points on the chewing surface of a back tooth called?
106230.e: Back teeth have a wide chewing surface with several cusps. They grind food as if between two millstones.
106230.m: The cusps of the back teeth grind food.

106231.q: What does the dentist do when sealing fissures?
a: She fills the grooves of the chewing surface with plastic
She pulls out a milk tooth
She glues a wire onto the teeth
106231.e: In sealing, the deep grooves of the back teeth are closed with runny plastic. Then bacteria can no longer settle there.
106231.m: Fissure sealing protects the chewing surfaces from decay.

106232.q: What is an artificial cap placed over a badly damaged tooth called?
106232.e: If not enough healthy tooth is left, it is capped with an artificial crown. A bridge, on the other hand, spans a gap between teeth.
106232.m: An artificial crown protects a badly damaged tooth.

106233.q: Which part of the tooth sits in the jawbone and holds the tooth in place?
106233.e: The root sits out of sight in the jawbone. It anchors the tooth so that it does not wobble when you chew.
106233.m: The root anchors the tooth in the jaw.

106234.q: Which hard layer covers the outside of the root of a tooth?
106234.e: The root is not covered with enamel but with a thin, bone-like layer called cementum. The fibres that hold the tooth are anchored in it.
106234.m: The root of a tooth is covered with cementum.

106235.q: What is the hollow in the jawbone that a tooth root sits in called?
106235.e: Each tooth root sits in its own socket, which experts call an alveolus. The socket is part of the jawbone.
106235.m: Each tooth root sits in its own socket.

106236.q: How is a tooth fixed in its socket?
a: With many fine fibres of the root lining
Only by the pressure of the gum
With a kind of glue made of saliva
106236.e: Between the root and the bone lies a lining with thousands of collagen fibres. They cushion the pressure of chewing, which is why a healthy tooth can move just a tiny bit.
106236.m: Fine fibres hold the tooth springily in the jawbone.

106237.q: Why do large back teeth have several roots?
a: They have to withstand strong chewing pressure
So that they fall out more easily
106237.e: You grind food with your back teeth. Several roots spread the strong chewing pressure onto the jawbone.
106237.m: Several roots hold back teeth firmly when you chew.

106238.q: How do nerves and blood vessels get inside a tooth?
a: Through a small opening at the tip of the root
Through the enamel of the crown
Through the gaps between the teeth
106238.e: At the tip of each root there is a tiny opening. There, nerves and blood vessels enter the root canal.
106238.m: Nerves and blood vessels reach the tooth through the tip of the root.

106239.q: Which metal is an artificial tooth root, a dental implant, usually made of?
106239.e: Most dental implants are made of titanium. It is very well tolerated and grows firmly together with the jawbone.
106239.m: Dental implants are usually made of well-tolerated titanium.

106240.q: Why does a milk tooth that has fallen out have almost no root left?
a: Its root was broken down beforehand
Milk teeth never grow with a root
The root stays stuck in the jaw
The root is worn away by chewing
106240.e: When the permanent tooth moves up, the body gradually breaks down the root of the milk tooth. In the end only a little tissue holds the milk tooth, and it wobbles.
106240.m: Before the teeth change, the root of the milk tooth is broken down.

106241.q: Where is the neck of a tooth?
a: Where the crown meets the root
At the tip of the root
In the middle of the chewing surface
106241.e: The neck of the tooth is the narrow area between the crown and the root. In healthy teeth, it lies at the edge of the gum.
106241.m: The neck of the tooth joins the crown and the root.

106242.q: Which two hard substances meet on the outside at the neck of a tooth?
106242.e: The crown is covered with enamel, the root with cementum. The border between the two runs exactly at the neck of the tooth.
106242.m: At the neck of the tooth, the enamel ends and the cementum begins.

106243.q: Why are exposed tooth necks often sensitive to pain?
a: Because unprotected dentine is exposed there
Because especially thick enamel lies there
106243.e: At the neck of the tooth there is no protective enamel. If it is exposed, fine channels in the dentine pass stimuli straight to the nerve.
106243.m: Exposed tooth necks are sensitive because they have no enamel.

106244.q: Which stimulus most often makes sensitive tooth necks hurt?
a: Cold, for example when eating ice cream
Breathing in deeply through the nose
106244.e: Cold, but also sweet or sour things, changes the fluid in the channels of the dentine. This irritates the nerve and causes a short, sharp pain.
106244.m: Sensitive tooth necks react especially strongly to cold.

106245.q: What can cause tooth necks to become exposed?
a: Scrubbing too hard with a hard toothbrush
106245.e: If you scrub with a lot of pressure and a hard brush, you can push the gum back. Gum disease (periodontitis) also makes the gum shrink.
106245.m: Gentle brushing protects the gums and the tooth necks.

106246.q: Why does decay start more easily on an exposed tooth neck than on the crown?
a: Because cementum and dentine are softer than enamel
Because the tooth neck keeps growing back
106246.e: Cementum and dentine contain fewer minerals than tooth enamel. That is why acids from bacteria attack them faster.
106246.m: An exposed tooth neck is especially prone to decay.

106247.q: How do many toothpastes for sensitive teeth help?
a: They seal the fine channels in the dentine
106247.e: Special ingredients settle in the open channels of the dentine and seal them. Stimuli such as cold then reach the nerve less strongly.
106247.m: Toothpaste for sensitive teeth seals open channels in the dentine.

106248.q: How should you brush so that the tooth necks are not damaged?
a: Scrubbing sideways with a lot of pressure
106248.e: If you scrub sideways with a lot of pressure, you can rub notches into the tooth at the neck. Brushing gently with a soft brush protects teeth and gums.
106248.m: Gentle brushing protects the tooth necks.

106249.q: What is the hard substance called that lies under the enamel and makes up most of the tooth?
106249.e: Dentine makes up the main part of the tooth. In the crown it lies under the enamel, in the root under the cementum.
106249.m: Dentine makes up most of a tooth.

106251.q: How hard is dentine compared with tooth enamel and bone?
a: Softer than enamel but harder than bone
106251.e: Dentine contains about 70 per cent minerals, which is less than enamel but more than bone. In return, it is a little more elastic than enamel.
106251.m: In hardness, dentine lies between enamel and bone.

106252.q: What runs through dentine in large numbers?
106252.e: Dentine is crossed by countless tiny channels that reach the pulp. They contain extensions of the cells that make the dentine.
106252.m: Countless fine channels run through dentine.

106253.q: Why do teeth with exposed dentine often hurt when you eat something cold?
a: Fine channels in the dentine pass the stimulus to the tooth nerve
106253.e: Dentine is crossed by tiny channels that reach the pulp. Without the protective enamel, cold and sweet things quickly reach the nerve.

106254.e: Dentine is yellowish. Because enamel is see-through, the dentine helps give the tooth its shade.
106254.m: The yellowish dentine shows through the enamel.

106255.q: What is ivory, the material of elephants’ tusks, made of?
106255.e: Elephants’ tusks are greatly lengthened teeth. Their ivory is mainly made of dentine.
106255.m: Ivory is the dentine of elephant tusks.

106256.q: What happens to the space for the pulp over a lifetime?
a: It gets smaller because new dentine forms
It gets bigger because dentine disappears
It always stays exactly the same size
106256.e: Throughout life, the odontoblasts slowly make more dentine towards the inside. This makes the pulp chamber narrower with age.
106256.m: With age, new dentine makes the pulp chamber narrower.

106257.q: What is the soft tissue inside a tooth called?
106257.e: Inside every tooth lies the dental pulp, a soft tissue. It fills the pulp chamber in the crown and the root canals.
106257.m: The soft dental pulp lies inside the tooth.

106259.q: What does the dental pulp contain?
106259.e: The pulp is made of connective tissue with nerves and blood vessels. It supplies the tooth and reports stimuli such as cold or pain.
106259.m: Through the pulp, nerves and blood vessels keep the tooth alive.

106260.q: What do you often feel when the pulp is inflamed?
a: A rushing sound in the ears
106260.e: The pulp contains nerves. When it is inflamed, severe, throbbing toothache often follows.
106260.m: An inflamed pulp causes severe toothache.

106261.q: In what order does deep decay get into a tooth from the outside?
106261.e: Decay starts in the outer enamel and eats its way into the dentine. If it reaches the pulp, the pulp becomes inflamed.
106261.m: Decay eats its way from the enamel through the dentine to the pulp.

106262.q: What is the part of the pulp chamber that runs through the root of the tooth called?
106262.e: In each root, the pulp chamber continues as a narrow root canal. Nerves and vessels run through it to the tip of the root.
106262.m: Nerves and vessels run through the root canal into the root.

106263.q: What does the dentist remove during root canal treatment?
a: The whole tooth with its root
106263.e: In root canal treatment, the diseased pulp is removed from the root canals. Then the canals are cleaned and tightly filled, so the tooth is saved.
106263.m: Root canal treatment saves the tooth by removing the diseased pulp.

106264.q: How can you often recognise a tooth whose pulp has died?
106264.e: If the pulp dies, for example after an accident, waste substances build up in the dentine. The tooth then looks grey or brownish.
106264.m: A dead tooth often turns dark.

106265.q: What is the best way to clean the gaps between the teeth at the edge of the gum?
106265.e: A toothbrush hardly reaches the gaps. Dental floss removes plaque there and so protects the gums.
106265.m: Dental floss cleans the gaps between the teeth.

106266.q: What do healthy gums look like?
106266.e: Healthy gums are pale pink and firm and fit tightly around the tooth. Redness and swelling are signs of inflammation.
106266.m: Healthy gums are pale pink and firm.

106267.q: What helps most against inflamed gums?
a: Brushing thoroughly and using dental floss
106267.e: Inflamed gums are usually caused by plaque at the edge of the gum. If it is removed regularly, the gums usually heal again.
106267.m: Good tooth care helps against inflamed gums.

106268.q: What is a typical sign of inflamed gums?
a: Bleeding gums when brushing your teeth
106268.e: Inflamed gums are red, swollen and bleed easily, for example when brushing. Healthy gums do not normally bleed when you do this.
106268.m: Bleeding gums are often a sign of inflammation.

106269.q: What is the most common cause of inflamed gums?
a: A layer of bacteria at the edge of the gum
106269.e: If plaque at the edge of the gum is not removed thoroughly, the gum reacts with inflammation. Good oral hygiene prevents this.
106269.m: Plaque at the edge of the gum causes inflamed gums.

106270.q: Where does plaque get stuck especially easily?
a: In the gaps between the teeth
On the tip of the tongue
On the front of the front teeth
106270.e: The toothbrush finds it hard to reach between the teeth. That is why plaque easily builds up there and irritates the gums.
106270.m: Plaque easily gets stuck between the teeth.

106271.q: Can inflamed gums heal completely again?
a: Yes, usually with good oral hygiene
Only by pulling out the teeth
106271.e: Gum inflammation on its own can be reversed. If the plaque is removed regularly, the gums usually become healthy again within a few days to weeks.
106271.m: Gingivitis usually heals completely with good tooth care.

106272.q: What is the narrow groove between the tooth and the edge of the gum called?
106272.e: Between the tooth and the edge of the gum there is a shallow groove. With healthy gums, it is only a few millimetres deep.
106272.m: A narrow gum groove lies between the tooth and the gum.

a: An inflammation of the tissues that hold the teeth
An inflammation of the jaw joint
A hole in the tooth enamel
Teeth that are out of line
106273.e: In periodontitis, the tissues that hold the tooth in the jaw become inflamed. In everyday language it is often simply called gum disease.
106273.m: Periodontitis attacks what holds the teeth in place.

106274.q: What makes periodontitis different from simple gum inflammation?
a: It also breaks down the jawbone
It only affects the tooth enamel
106274.e: Gingivitis only affects the gums. In periodontitis, the fibres that hold the tooth and the jawbone are broken down as well, and these do not grow back by themselves.
106274.m: In periodontitis, jawbone is lost too.

106275.q: Which warning sign can point to inflammation of the gums?
a: Bleeding gums when brushing your teeth
106275.e: Healthy gums are firm and do not bleed. If they bleed when you brush, they are often inflamed, and this can turn into periodontitis.
106275.m: Bleeding gums are a warning sign.

106276.e: Bacteria from plaque on and below the edge of the gum trigger the inflammation. The body’s defence reaction also destroys tissue in the process.
106276.m: Bacteria in plaque are the main cause of periodontitis.

106277.q: What can happen if periodontitis is not treated?
a: The teeth become loose and fall out
The teeth become longer and stronger
106277.e: As more and more bone is broken down, the teeth lose their hold. In adults, periodontitis is a common cause of losing teeth.
106277.m: Untreated periodontitis can lead to losing teeth.

106278.q: Which habit clearly increases the risk of periodontitis?
106278.e: Smoking reduces the blood supply to the gums and weakens the body’s defences. Smokers get periodontitis much more often.
106278.m: Smoking harms the gums and encourages periodontitis.

106279.q: What does the dentist measure with a fine probe to detect periodontitis?
a: The depth of the gum pockets
106279.e: In periodontitis, the gum comes away from the tooth and deep pockets form. Their depth is measured in millimetres with a probe.
106279.m: Deep gum pockets are a sign of periodontitis.

106280.q: With which general illness is the risk of periodontitis higher?
106280.e: People with diabetes mellitus get periodontitis more often and more severely. In turn, periodontitis can make blood sugar harder to control.
106280.m: Diabetes and periodontitis affect each other.

106281.q: What is the branch of dentistry called that treats crooked teeth with braces?
106281.e: Orthodontics corrects crooked teeth and bites that do not meet properly. The specialists are called orthodontists.
106281.m: Orthodontists straighten crooked teeth with braces.

106282.q: In fixed braces, what connects the brackets to each other?
106282.e: A springy archwire runs through all the brackets. It applies gentle pressure and slowly moves the teeth into the desired position.
106282.m: The archwire of the brace slowly pushes the teeth into place.

106283.q: What are the clear plastic trays called that can straighten teeth without brackets?
106283.e: Aligners are almost invisible trays that are replaced by new ones every few weeks. Each tray moves the teeth a little further.
106283.m: Aligners are clear trays that move teeth step by step.

106284.q: What is a retainer for after treatment with a brace?
a: It holds the teeth in their new position
106284.e: After treatment, teeth often want to move back to where they were. A retainer, such as a thin wire behind the teeth, prevents this.
106284.m: A retainer keeps the result of the brace.

106285.q: Why can teeth be moved with a brace at all?
a: The jawbone breaks down on the pressure side and builds up on the pulling side
The teeth become as soft as rubber
The roots come away from the tooth
The wire makes the jaw grow faster
106285.e: Constant light pressure means bone in front of the tooth is broken down and new bone forms behind it. So the tooth slowly travels through the bone.
106285.m: Teeth move because the jawbone reshapes itself under pressure.

106286.q: Which kind of brace can you take out of your mouth yourself?
106286.e: A removable brace is made of a plastic plate with wires and is taken out for eating. But it only works if you wear it for long enough.
106286.m: A removable brace only works if you wear it regularly.

106287.q: Why is thorough brushing especially important with fixed braces?
a: Plaque easily gets stuck on the brackets
Otherwise the wire rusts straight away
Otherwise the teeth grow too fast
106287.e: Food scraps and bacteria collect around the brackets and wire. Without thorough care, white decay spots and inflamed gums are a risk.
106287.m: Fixed braces need especially thorough tooth care.

106288.q: Which tooth is the wisdom tooth?
106288.e: The wisdom tooth is the very back tooth in each row. Experts call it the third molar.
106288.m: The wisdom tooth is the last large back tooth.

106289.q: How many wisdom teeth does a complete set of permanent teeth have?
106289.e: A complete set of permanent teeth has 32 teeth. In each of the four quarters of the jaw, there is a wisdom tooth at the back.
106289.m: A complete set of teeth has four wisdom teeth.

106290.q: When do wisdom teeth usually come through?
a: In the late teens or early adulthood
106290.e: Wisdom teeth are the last teeth to appear, often between about 16 and 25. In some people they never come through.
106290.m: Wisdom teeth come last, often only in early adulthood.

106291.q: Where does the wisdom tooth get its name from?
a: It only comes when you are older and supposedly wiser
It was discovered by a scholar called Wisdom
It sits right under the brain
106291.e: Because the tooth appears late, when you are already grown up, it was called the wisdom tooth. It has nothing to do with cleverness.
106291.m: The wisdom tooth is called that because it comes through late.

106292.q: Why do wisdom teeth often have to be removed?
a: Because there is too little room for them in the jaw
106292.e: Often there is not enough room in the jaw. The teeth then stay stuck at an angle in the bone, press on neighbouring teeth or become inflamed.
106292.m: There is often not enough room in the jaw for wisdom teeth.

106293.q: Do all people have wisdom teeth forming?
a: No, some people are missing some or all of them
Yes, every single person has all four
106293.e: In many people, one or more wisdom teeth never form at all. This is harmless.

106294.q: What is a wisdom tooth called that lies at an angle in the jaw and cannot come through properly?
106294.e: If there is no room, the wisdom tooth often tilts and stays wholly or partly stuck in the bone. This is called an impacted tooth.
106294.m: An impacted wisdom tooth stays stuck at an angle in the jaw.

106295.q: How many teeth does a complete set of permanent teeth with wisdom teeth have?
106295.e: The permanent set has 32 teeth, four of them wisdom teeth. The set of milk teeth has only 20 teeth.
106295.m: A complete set of permanent teeth has 32 teeth.

a: It hardens tooth enamel and protects against decay
It makes the gums grow back
106296.e: Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to acids. This makes it one of the most important protective substances against decay.
106296.m: Fluoride in toothpaste protects the teeth from decay.

106297.q: How does fluoride act on early, still small spots of decay?
a: It helps minerals to be stored again
It eats the bacteria up straight away
It fills the hole with plastic
106297.e: Fluoride encourages remineralisation, which means calcium and phosphate are stored in the enamel again. In this way, early loss of minerals can heal.
106297.m: Fluoride helps enamel to store lost minerals again.

106298.q: Which food is widely enriched with fluoride in Switzerland?
106298.e: Switzerland has had fluoridated table salt for decades. It is used at home and by many bakeries and restaurants.
106298.m: In Switzerland, table salt is often enriched with fluoride.

106299.q: How often a day should you brush your teeth with fluoride toothpaste?
106299.e: Dentists recommend brushing with fluoride toothpaste at least twice a day, ideally in the morning and evening.
106299.m: Brushing twice a day protects the teeth.

106300.q: What can too much fluoride cause in children while their teeth are developing?
a: White spots in the tooth enamel
106300.e: If too much fluoride is taken in over a long time while the teeth are forming, dental fluorosis can develop. It usually shows as white spots or streaks.
106300.m: Too much fluoride can cause white spots on children’s teeth.

106301.q: Which chemical element does fluoride come from?
106301.e: Fluorides are compounds of the element fluorine. Fluorine itself is a very reactive, poisonous gas, but fluorides in small amounts protect the teeth.
106301.m: Fluorides are compounds of the element fluorine.

106302.q: What is recommended after brushing your teeth so that the fluoride works better?
a: Just spit out the foam, do not rinse hard
Drink a glass of orange juice straight away
Rinse your teeth with hot water
106302.e: If you rinse hard with water after brushing, you also rinse away the fluoride. Just spitting out leaves more of it working on your teeth.
106302.m: Spitting out instead of rinsing after brushing lets the fluoride work for longer.

106303.q: Which fluoride treatment does the dentist put directly on the teeth?
106303.e: Fluoride varnish is painted onto the teeth at the dentist’s. It sticks for a few hours and releases a lot of fluoride into the enamel.
106303.m: Fluoride varnish is painted onto the teeth at the dentist’s.

106304.q: Apart from hardening the enamel, what other protective effect does fluoride have?
a: It slows down the production of acid by bacteria
It kills all the viruses in the mouth
106304.e: Fluoride interferes with the metabolism of decay bacteria. As a result, they make less acid from sugar.
106304.m: Fluoride slows down acid production by decay bacteria.

106305.q: What is plaque on the teeth?
a: A hard layer of tooth enamel
106305.e: Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria, the substances they produce and food scraps. It forms again every day.
106305.m: Plaque is a soft layer of bacteria on the teeth.

106306.q: How does plaque lead to tooth decay?
a: Bacteria make acids from sugar that remove minerals from the enamel
Plaque sucks water out of the tooth
Plaque grows into the tooth like a root
106306.e: The bacteria in plaque use sugar and give off acids as they do so. These dissolve minerals out of the enamel until a hole forms.
106306.m: Acids from plaque dissolve tooth enamel.

106307.q: What forms if plaque is not removed for a long time and hardens?
106307.e: Minerals from saliva build up in the plaque. This makes it hard, and then it can only be removed at the dentist’s.

106308.q: How can you make plaque on the teeth visible?
106308.e: Disclosing tablets or solutions colour the plaque red or blue. This shows exactly where you have not yet brushed thoroughly.
106308.m: Disclosing tablets show where plaque is still sitting.

106309.q: Why is brushing your teeth before going to sleep especially important?
a: During sleep little saliva flows to buffer acids
Teeth grow at night and need room
Enamel becomes as soft as rubber during sleep
The mouth makes more sugar at night
106309.e: During sleep the body makes only a little saliva. Acids from plaque can then work on the teeth undisturbed for a long time.
106309.m: Plaque should be removed thoroughly before going to sleep.

106310.q: In biology, what is plaque described as?
106310.e: Plaque is a biofilm, a community of microorganisms that stick to a surface in a slimy layer. Biofilms like this are also found on stones in a stream.
106310.m: Plaque is a biofilm made of many bacteria.

106311.q: Why is snacking often throughout the day especially bad for your teeth?
a: Every time you eat sugar, a new acid attack starts
Sugar makes saliva sweet and sticky like glue
106311.e: After each time you eat sugar, the bacteria produce acid for a while. If you snack all the time, the saliva has no time to neutralise the acid.
106311.m: Snacking less often gives your teeth a rest from acid attacks.

106312.q: How does saliva protect the teeth from the acids in plaque?
a: It neutralises acids and supplies minerals
106312.e: Saliva buffers acids and contains calcium and phosphate. With these it can partly repair damaged enamel.
106312.m: Saliva neutralises acids and so protects tooth enamel.

106313.q: Which drink is best for your teeth?
106313.e: Squash, fruit juice and iced tea contain lots of sugar. The bacteria in plaque turn it into acid, which harms the teeth. Water has no sugar.
106313.m: Water is the most tooth-friendly drink for quenching thirst.

106314.e: If plaque stays on the teeth for a longer time, minerals build up in it and it hardens. This creates firm tartar.

106315.q: Where do the minerals that harden plaque into tartar come from?
a: From the blood in the gums
106315.e: Saliva contains dissolved calcium and phosphate. These substances settle in the plaque and make it hard.
106315.m: Minerals from saliva turn plaque into tartar.

106316.q: Where does tartar form especially often?
a: On the inside of the lower front teeth
On the chewing surface of the wisdom teeth
On the tip of the tongue
On the outside of the lower canines
106316.e: Large salivary glands open under the tongue. That is why especially a lot of tartar builds up on the inside of the lower front teeth.
106316.m: Especially a lot of tartar forms behind the lower front teeth.

106317.q: Can you remove hard tartar yourself with a toothbrush?
a: No, a professional has to do it at the practice
Yes, with lots of dental floss
106317.e: Tartar sticks so firmly that a brush and floss are not enough. It is removed with special instruments at the dental practice.
106317.m: Only a professional at the practice can remove tartar.

106318.q: In Switzerland, which professional often removes tartar during regular teeth cleaning?
106318.e: Dental hygienists specialise in professional teeth cleaning. They remove tartar and plaque and give advice on oral hygiene.
106318.m: The dental hygienist removes tartar during teeth cleaning.

106319.q: Which device is often used to remove tartar?
106319.e: An ultrasonic device makes a fine tip vibrate very quickly. The vibrations loosen the hard deposit without damaging the tooth.
106319.m: An ultrasonic device shakes tartar off the teeth.

106320.q: Why is tartar harmful even though it does not make a hole in the tooth itself?
a: New plaque sticks especially well to its rough surface
It is so heavy that the teeth break
It sends electrical signals to the nerve
106320.e: Tartar is rough and porous. New plaque keeps settling on it and inflames the gums.
106320.m: Tartar encourages inflamed gums because new plaque sticks to it.

106321.q: Why does tartar often turn dark in smokers or tea drinkers?
a: Colourings settle in its porous surface
It rusts because of the oxygen
It burns because of the heat
It takes on the colour of the gums
106321.e: The rough, porous surface of tartar soaks up colourings from tobacco, tea or coffee. This turns it yellowish to brown.
106321.m: Tartar soaks up colourings from tea, coffee and tobacco.

106322.q: How does tartar below the edge of the gum usually differ from tartar above it?
a: It is darker and sticks more firmly
106322.e: Tartar under the gum takes up blood pigments and therefore looks dark. It is very hard, sits firmly on the root and encourages periodontitis.
106322.m: Tartar under the gum is dark and especially stubborn.

106618.q: Where does the right atrium pass its blood on to?
106618.e: The right atrium contracts and pushes the blood through a valve into the right ventricle below it.
106618.m: Each atrium passes its blood to the ventricle on the same side.

106619.q: What is the technical term for one of the two upper chambers of the heart?
106619.e: In technical language, an upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium, the Latin word for entrance hall. Doctors speak of the right and left atrium.
106619.m: An upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium.

106620.q: Why do the atria have thinner muscle walls than the ventricles?
a: They only push the blood into the nearby ventricle.
They contain no blood at all.
106620.e: The atria only have to move the blood a short distance into the ventricles. This needs little force and so little muscle.
106620.m: The atria need little force and so have thin walls.

106621.q: What is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, in which the atria twitch irregularly, called?
106621.e: In atrial fibrillation, the atria no longer contract in an orderly way. It is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, especially in older people.
106621.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder.

106622.q: Why does only a little blood flow through the lungs of an unborn baby?
a: Because it does not breathe yet and gets oxygen through the umbilical cord
Because it has no lungs yet
Because its heart does not beat yet
106622.e: Before birth, the baby gets oxygen through the umbilical cord. That is why most of the blood bypasses the lungs, partly through an opening between the atria.
106622.m: Before birth, most of the blood bypasses the lungs.

106624.q: Roughly how much blood does one ventricle of an adult pump out per heartbeat at rest?
106624.e: This stroke volume is around 70 millilitres at rest, which is about as much as five tablespoons. During sport it can rise a lot.
106624.m: Each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per heartbeat.

106625.q: What is the sac of connective tissue that surrounds the whole heart called?
106625.e: The pericardium surrounds the heart like a cover. A thin layer of fluid inside it lets the heart glide smoothly as it beats.
106625.m: The pericardium protects the heart and lets it beat smoothly.

106626.q: How many valves does the human heart have?
106626.e: There are two valves between the atria and the ventricles and two at the exits of the ventricles. Together that makes four.

106627.q: What do you mainly hear when listening to the heart with a stethoscope?
a: The lungs rushing inside the heart
106627.e: The typical heart sounds are made when the heart valves close. In this way doctors can hear whether the valves are working properly.
106627.m: Heart sounds are made when the heart valves close.

106628.q: In which direction do the valves between atrium and ventricle let the blood flow?
a: From the atrium into the ventricle
From the ventricle into the atrium
Not at all, they are always shut
106628.e: The atria collect the blood and pass it on to the ventricles. The valves between them only let it through in this direction.
106628.m: Blood flows from the atrium into the ventricle.

106630.q: What makes the heart valves open and close?
a: Their own muscles in the valves
106630.e: Heart valves move without any force of their own. When blood pushes from one side they open, and when it pushes back they shut like a door in the wind.
106630.m: Blood pressure opens and closes the heart valves.

106631.q: What stops the flap valves from flipping back into the atria when the ventricles contract?
106631.e: Fine tendon cords connect the flaps to small muscles in the wall of the ventricle. They hold the flaps in place like the lines of a parachute.
106631.m: Tendon cords hold the flap valves in position.

106633.q: What is the curved section of the aorta just above the heart called?
106633.e: The aorta first rises upwards and then bends backwards and downwards in an arch. The arteries for the head and arms branch off from the aortic arch.
106633.m: The aortic arch lies just above the heart.

106634.q: Which vessels are the first to branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself?
106634.e: The coronary arteries branch off just after the aortic valve. They lie around the heart like a crown and supply it with oxygen.
106634.m: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood.

106635.q: What kind of blood flows in the aorta?
106635.e: The blood in the aorta comes straight from the heart after it has picked up fresh oxygen in the lungs. That is why it is rich in oxygen.
106635.m: Oxygen-rich blood flows in the aorta.

106636.q: Why is the aorta the largest artery in the body?
a: All the blood from the left ventricle flows through it
It brings blood back to the heart
It carries air to the lungs
106636.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. All the arteries of the body’s circulation branch off from it.
106636.m: The aorta is the largest artery in the body.

106637.q: How many venae cavae lead into the heart?
106637.e: There is a superior (upper) and an inferior (lower) vena cava. Both bring blood from the body to the heart.
106637.m: An upper and a lower vena cava lead to the heart.

106638.q: Which chamber of the heart do the venae cavae lead into?
106638.e: Both venae cavae end in the right atrium. That is where the blood’s journey to the lungs begins.
106638.m: The venae cavae lead into the right atrium.

106639.q: From which parts of the body does the superior vena cava collect blood?
a: From the head, neck and arms
106639.e: The superior vena cava brings the blood back from the upper half of the body. This includes the head, neck and arms.
106639.m: The superior vena cava brings blood back from the head and arms.

106640.q: From which areas of the body does the blood in the inferior vena cava come?
106640.e: The inferior vena cava collects the blood from the lower body. It runs up next to the spine to the heart.
106640.m: The inferior vena cava brings blood back from the legs and abdomen.

106641.q: What kind of blood do the venae cavae carry?
106641.e: The blood has given up its oxygen to the organs before it reaches the venae cavae. That is why it is low in oxygen and darker.
106641.m: Used, oxygen-poor blood flows in the venae cavae.

106642.q: Which is the largest vein in the human body?
106642.e: The inferior vena cava has the largest diameter of all veins. It carries the blood of the whole lower half of the body.
106642.m: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body.

106643.q: Where do the venae cavae take the blood?
106643.e: The superior and inferior venae cavae collect the blood from the body and take it back to the heart.
106643.m: The venae cavae take the blood back to the heart.

106644.q: What is the pulmonary circulation also called?
106644.e: The pulmonary circulation only goes from the heart to the lungs and back. Because the route is short, it is called the small circulation.
106644.m: The pulmonary circulation is the small circulation.

106645.q: In which chamber of the heart does the pulmonary circulation begin?
106645.e: The right ventricle pumps the oxygen-poor blood towards the lungs. That is where the pulmonary circulation begins.
106645.m: The pulmonary circulation begins in the right ventricle.

106646.q: Where does the pulmonary circulation end?
106646.e: The fresh blood flows from the lungs back to the heart and reaches the left atrium there. This closes the small circulation.
106646.m: The pulmonary circulation ends in the left atrium.

106647.q: How does blood pressure in the pulmonary circulation compare with the body’s circulation?
106647.e: The lungs are close to the heart, and the delicate air sacs cannot cope with high pressure. That is why the pressure in the pulmonary circulation is much lower.
106647.m: Blood pressure is low in the pulmonary circulation.

106648.q: Which blood vessels bring the blood from the lungs back to the heart?
106648.e: After the exchange of gases, the pulmonary veins collect the fresh blood. They take it back to the heart.
106648.m: The pulmonary veins bring fresh blood from the lungs to the heart.

106649.q: What is the body’s circulation (systemic circulation) also called?
106649.e: The body’s circulation supplies the whole body from head to toe. Because it reaches so far, it is called the large circulation.
106649.m: The body’s circulation is the large circulation.

106650.q: In which chamber of the heart does the body’s circulation begin?
106650.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the body. From there it spreads to all the organs.
106650.m: The body’s circulation begins in the left ventricle.

106651.q: What happens to the ventricles during systole?
a: They contract and pump blood out.
106651.e: During systole, the muscles of the ventricles contract. This pushes the blood into the large arteries.
106651.m: In systole, the ventricles pump the blood out.

106652.q: Where do the ventricles pump the blood during systole?
a: Into the large arteries such as the aorta
106652.e: The ventricles contract and push the blood into the large arteries. Valves stop it from flowing back into the atria.
106652.m: In systole, the blood flows into the arteries.

106653.q: What does the Greek word “systole” literally mean?
106653.e: Systole comes from Greek and means contraction. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase.

106654.q: What happens to the ventricles during diastole?
a: They relax and fill with blood.
They push blood into the aorta.
106654.e: Diastole is the phase of relaxing and filling. The muscles of the ventricles relax, and blood flows in from the atria.
106654.m: In diastole, the ventricles relax and fill.

106655.q: Where does the blood flow into the ventricles from while they relax in diastole?
106655.e: During diastole, the flap valves open. So blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.
106655.m: In diastole, blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.

106656.q: What is the phase called in which the ventricles contract and push blood out?
106656.e: In systole, the ventricles contract and pump blood into the arteries. In diastole, they relax and fill again.
106656.m: Systole means pumping, diastole means relaxing and filling.

106657.q: Which reading when measuring blood pressure belongs to diastole?
106657.e: In 120 over 80, the 80 is the diastolic reading. It shows the pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes.
106657.m: The lower blood pressure reading is the diastolic one.

106658.q: Which phase lasts longer in a calm heartbeat?
a: Neither, there is only one phase
106658.e: At rest, the relaxing and filling phase takes up about two thirds of a heartbeat. This gives the ventricles enough time to fill.
106658.m: At rest, diastole lasts longer than systole.

106659.q: What happens during a heart attack?
a: A blood vessel of the heart gets blocked and part of the heart muscle gets no oxygen
The heart suddenly becomes twice as big
106659.e: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood. If one of them closes, the affected part of the heart muscle dies without quick help.
106659.m: In a heart attack, part of the heart muscle lacks oxygen.

106660.q: What is a stent, which is often used after a heart attack?
a: A small mesh tube that holds a vessel open
106660.e: A stent is pushed into the narrowed vessel with a catheter and widened there. It supports the vessel wall so that the blood can flow again.
106660.m: A stent holds a narrowed vessel open.

106661.q: What is a defibrillator used for?
a: To stop a dangerous heart rhythm with an electric shock
To blow oxygen into the lungs
106661.e: A defibrillator gives a strong electric shock. This can stop a chaotic heart rhythm so that the heart can beat normally again.
106661.m: A defibrillator uses electricity to stop a life-threatening heart rhythm.

106662.q: What does the abbreviation AED stand for?
106662.e: An AED is a device for ordinary people that analyses the heart rhythm by itself. In Switzerland, devices like this hang in many railway stations, schools and sports grounds.
106662.m: An AED is an automatic defibrillator for everyone.

106663.q: Which heart rhythm disorder can be stopped with a defibrillator?
106663.e: In ventricular fibrillation, the ventricles twitch chaotically and no longer pump blood. An electric shock can end this chaos.
106663.m: Ventricular fibrillation is life-threatening and is treated with a defibrillator.

106664.q: Can a person with no medical training use an AED?
a: Yes, the device gives spoken instructions.
106664.e: An AED explains every step with spoken instructions. It only gives a shock if it detects a suitable rhythm.
106664.m: Anyone may and should use an AED in an emergency.

106665.q: Where do you stick the pads of an AED?
a: On the soles of the feet
On the back over the clothes
106665.e: The sticky pads go on the bare skin of the upper body. The pads have a picture showing exactly where they belong.
106665.m: You stick the pads of an AED on the bare chest.

106666.q: What must you remember while the AED gives a shock?
a: You must hold the person tight.
You must pour water over the chest.
106666.e: Otherwise the electric shock could also pass to the helpers. That is why the device tells everyone to stand clear.
106666.m: Nobody touches the person during the shock.

106667.q: How fast should you press during chest compressions?
106667.e: The guidelines recommend a rate of 100 to 120 compressions a minute. That is about the beat of a fast pop song.
106667.m: In chest compressions you press 100 to 120 times a minute.

106668.q: How deep should you press down an adult’s chest during chest compressions?
a: Not at all, just touch it
106668.e: For effective chest compressions, the chest is pressed down about 5 to 6 centimetres. Only then is enough blood pushed around the body.
106668.m: In adults you press the chest down about five to six centimetres.

106669.q: What is a defibrillator placed under the skin called?
106669.e: An implantable defibrillator, ICD for short, constantly monitors the heart rhythm. If ventricular fibrillation happens, it gives a shock by itself.
106669.m: An implantable defibrillator watches over the heart around the clock.

a: In the wall of the right atrium
106670.e: The sinus node is a small group of special heart muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium. Every normal heartbeat starts there.
106670.m: The sinus node is in the right atrium.

106671.q: What job does the sinus node have in the heart?
a: It sets the rhythm of the heartbeat
106671.e: The sinus node sends out electrical impulses regularly. Each impulse triggers a heartbeat, which is why it is called the heart’s pacemaker.
106671.m: The sinus node is the heart’s pacemaker.

106672.q: What is put in when the heart’s natural pacemaker no longer works properly?
106672.e: A pacemaker is a small device under the skin. It gives electrical impulses when the heart beats too slowly.
106672.m: A pacemaker replaces a weak natural pacemaker.

106673.q: How does the resting pulse often change in well-trained endurance athletes?
a: It is lower than in untrained people.
It goes up and down a lot for no reason.
106673.e: A trained heart pumps more blood with each beat. That is why it needs fewer beats at rest, often under 60 a minute.
106673.m: Training can lower the resting pulse.

106674.q: Which signs of a heart attack appear more often in women than in men?
a: Nausea, shortness of breath and back pain
106674.e: In women, the typical chest pain is missing more often. Instead, nausea, shortness of breath or pain in the back or upper abdomen appear more often.
106674.m: A heart attack can also happen without chest pain.

106675.q: What can a biological replacement heart valve be made from?
106675.e: Biological heart valves are often made from tissue from pigs or cattle. There are also mechanical valves made of metal and plastic.
106675.m: Replacement heart valves are made of animal tissue or metal.

106676.q: What is the section of the aorta below the diaphragm called?
106676.e: The aorta passes through an opening in the diaphragm into the abdomen. There it is called the abdominal aorta and sends branches to the intestines and kidneys.
106676.m: Below the diaphragm, the aorta is called the abdominal aorta.

106677.q: Which part of the heart contracts first with every heartbeat?
106677.e: The electrical signal starts at the top of the heart. That is why the atria contract first and top up the filling of the ventricles, and only then do the ventricles follow.
106677.m: With every heartbeat, the atria contract first.

106678.q: How many atria does the human heart have?
106678.e: The heart has a right and a left atrium. Below each one lies a ventricle.
106678.m: The heart has two atria and two ventricles.

106679.q: What do the atria do while the ventricles contract?
a: They fill with blood from the veins.
They pump blood into the aorta.
106679.e: While the ventricles pump out blood, the atria are relaxed. During this time, new blood is already flowing into them from the veins.
106679.m: The atria fill up while the ventricles pump.

106680.q: A heart pumps 70 ml of blood per beat and beats 70 times a minute. Roughly how much blood does it pump per minute?
106680.e: 70 times 70 ml makes 4900 ml, so almost 5 litres. That is about all the blood of an adult going once round the body every minute.
106680.m: At rest the heart pumps about 5 litres of blood a minute.

106681.q: What is a congenital heart defect?
a: A fault in the heart that is already there at birth
A heart attack in old age
A pulse that is too fast after sport
A cold that affects the heart
106681.e: Congenital heart defects develop while the heart is growing in the womb. One example is a hole in the wall between the ventricles. Many can be treated well today.
106681.m: A congenital heart defect is already there at birth.

106682.q: What is the wall of the ventricles mainly made of?
106682.e: The wall of the heart is mainly made of heart muscle. When it contracts, the blood is pushed out of the ventricles.
106682.m: The ventricles are surrounded by strong muscles.

106683.q: Why is the inside of the ventricles completely smooth?
a: So that the blood flows freely and does not clot
So that the heart is lighter
So that you can hear the heart beating
106683.e: A thin, smooth lining covers the chambers and valves of the heart. Blood clots could form more easily on rough spots.
106683.m: The smooth inner lining of the heart helps the blood flow well.

106684.q: What share of the blood in a healthy left ventricle is pumped out with each heartbeat?
106684.e: A healthy left ventricle pumps out about 55 to 70 per cent of its contents with each beat. This share is called the ejection fraction.
106684.m: A healthy ventricle pumps out more than half its blood with each beat.

106685.q: Where does the blood flow when the valve at the exit of the left ventricle opens?
106685.e: The aortic valve sits at the exit of the left ventricle. When it opens, oxygen-rich blood flows into the aorta and from there to the whole body.
106685.m: From the left ventricle, the blood flows into the aorta.

106686.q: What does the heart have to do if a heart valve is narrowed and no longer opens wide?
106686.e: Blood can only be pushed through a narrow opening with more force. In the long run this overloads the heart muscle, which is why severe narrowing is treated.
106686.m: With a narrowed valve, the heart has to work harder.

106687.q: What happens if a heart valve leaks?
a: Some of the blood flows back
106687.e: A leaky valve does not close completely. Some of the blood flows back, and the heart has to pump it again.
106687.m: With a leaky valve, blood flows back.

106688.q: Which large arteries that supply the head branch off from the aortic arch?
106688.e: Large branches go upwards from the aortic arch. From them come the carotid arteries for the head and brain and the arteries for the arms.
106688.m: The carotid arteries get their blood from the aortic arch.

106689.q: Roughly where does the aorta split into the two pelvic arteries?
a: At about the level of the belly button
106689.e: The aorta runs downwards in front of the spine. At about the level of the belly button, it forks into a left and a right pelvic artery.
106689.m: The aorta forks at about the level of the belly button.

106690.q: How does the blood pressure in the venae cavae near the heart compare with the aorta?
106690.e: On its long journey through arteries and capillaries, the blood loses almost all its pressure. That is why the pressure in the venae cavae near the heart is very low.
106690.m: Blood pressure in the venae cavae is very low.

106691.q: What is the large vessel called that comes out of the right ventricle and splits into a left and a right pulmonary artery?
106691.e: The pulmonary trunk comes out of the right ventricle. Shortly afterwards it splits into one artery for each lung.
106691.m: The pulmonary trunk splits into a left and a right pulmonary artery.

106692.q: Which Arab doctor was the first to describe the pulmonary circulation, in the 13th century?
106692.e: Ibn al-Nafis lived in Damascus and Cairo. He realised that blood travels from the right half of the heart through the lungs to the left half.
106692.m: Ibn al-Nafis described the pulmonary circulation in the 13th century.

106693.q: How many pulmonary veins normally lead into the human heart?
106693.e: Usually two pulmonary veins come from each lung. So together there are normally four.
106693.m: Normally four pulmonary veins lead to the heart.

106694.q: Why do we talk about the blood’s “circulation”?
a: The blood keeps flowing back to the heart
The blood flows in a circle around the tummy
106694.e: The heart pumps the blood through the arteries into the body. Through the veins it flows back to the heart, and everything starts again.
106694.m: The blood flows in a circle away from the heart and back again.

106695.q: What are the finest blood vessels, where oxygen is passed to the cells, called?
106695.e: Capillaries are thinner than a hair. Oxygen and nutrients reach the cells through their thin walls.
106695.m: In the capillaries, the blood passes oxygen to the cells.

106696.q: What share of all the blood is in the veins at rest?
106696.e: Veins are wide and stretchy and work like a blood store. Around two thirds of the blood is in them.
106696.m: The veins hold most of the blood.

106697.q: Which pair of organs receives about a fifth of the blood pumped out by the heart at rest?
106697.e: The kidneys constantly filter the blood and so have a very large blood supply. They get around 20 per cent of the heart’s output, even though they are small.
106697.m: The kidneys have an especially large blood supply.

106698.q: What happens to the small arteries in the skin in the cold?
106698.e: Narrowed skin vessels let less warm blood reach the surface of the body. So the body loses less heat, and the skin turns pale.
106698.m: In the cold, the blood vessels in the skin narrow.

106699.q: What is the phase after systole called, in which the heart relaxes and fills with blood?
106699.e: The heart switches between systole and diastole. In systole it pumps, in diastole it relaxes and fills again.

106700.q: What is the phase of systole called in which blood flows out of the ventricles?
106700.e: As soon as the pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the artery, the valve opens. Now the blood is pushed out.
106700.m: In the ejection phase, blood flows out of the ventricles.

106701.q: Which heart sound can be heard at the start of systole?
106701.e: At the start of systole, the flap valves close and the heart muscle tenses. This makes the first heart sound.
106701.m: The first heart sound marks the start of systole.

106702.e: In an extrasystole, the heart beats outside its normal rhythm. Single extrasystoles are common and usually harmless.
106702.m: An extrasystole is a heartbeat outside the normal rhythm.

106703.q: When is the pressure in the aorta highest?
106703.e: When the left ventricle pumps out blood, the pressure in the aorta rises to its highest value. Then it falls again until the next heartbeat.
106703.m: The pressure in the aorta is highest during systole.

106704.q: What do the ventricles do straight after diastole?
a: They stand still for a minute
106704.e: The filling phase is followed by systole. The ventricles contract and pump the blood into the body and the lungs.
106704.m: Diastole is always followed by systole.

106705.q: What does the Greek word “diastole” literally mean?
106705.e: Diastole comes from Greek and means expansion. In this phase the ventricles widen and take in blood.

106706.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland if you suspect a heart attack?
106706.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 145 Tox Info Suisse for poisoning.
106706.m: If you suspect a heart attack, call 144 straight away.

106707.q: Which examination uses contrast dye to show narrowed coronary arteries?
106707.e: A thin tube is pushed along an artery up to the heart. With contrast dye and X-rays, doctors can see exactly where a vessel is narrowed.
106707.m: Cardiac catheterisation finds narrowed coronary arteries.

106708.q: What is the operation called in which a blocked coronary artery is bypassed with a piece of vessel?
106708.e: In a bypass, a piece of vein or artery is sewn on as a detour. So the blood flows past the blocked spot.
106708.m: A bypass is a detour around a blocked heart vessel.

106709.q: Which metabolic illness with permanently raised blood sugar increases the risk of a heart attack?
106709.e: Permanently high blood sugar damages the walls of the blood vessels. That is why people with diabetes have a higher risk of heart attacks.
106709.m: Diabetes damages the vessels and increases the risk of a heart attack.

106710.q: What do you count when you take a pulse?
a: How often the heart beats per minute
How often you breathe per minute
106710.e: With every heartbeat you feel a push in the arteries. If you count these pushes for one minute, you know the heart rate.
106710.m: The pulse shows how often the heart beats per minute.

106711.q: What happens to the pulse with a fever or great excitement?
a: It always stays exactly the same
106711.e: With a fever, excitement or exertion, the sinus node makes the heart beat faster. This gives the body more blood and oxygen.
106711.m: Fever and excitement make the pulse faster.

106712.q: How does the heartbeat normally change during sleep?
106712.e: During sleep, the body needs less energy. Nerves then slow down the sinus node, and the heart beats more calmly.
106712.m: The heart beats more slowly during sleep.

106713.q: How does the signal from the sinus node reach the ventricles?
a: As an electrical signal along special fibres
With the blood through the vessels
106713.e: The heart has its own conduction system. Special muscle fibres pass the electrical signal from the sinus node to the ventricles.
106713.m: The heart passes on its rhythm electrically.

106714.q: Which phase mainly gets shorter when the heart beats faster during sport?
106714.e: With a high pulse, it is mainly the filling phase that gets shorter. The pumping phase, by contrast, stays almost the same length.
106714.m: When the heart beats fast, it is mainly diastole that gets shorter.

106715.q: What is a typical sign of a heart attack?
a: Severe pain or pressure in the chest
106715.e: A typical sign is severe pain or pressure behind the breastbone. It can spread to the left arm, the neck or the jaw.
106715.m: Severe chest pain can be a warning sign of a heart attack.

106716.q: How should a person with a suspected heart attack behave until the ambulance arrives?
a: Sit calmly with the upper body raised
106716.e: Rest and a raised upper body take strain off the heart. Any effort increases the oxygen needs of the damaged heart muscle.
106716.m: With a suspected heart attack, the person should sit calmly with the upper body raised.

106717.q: What happens to the blood vessels in working muscles during sport?
106717.e: Working muscles need much more oxygen. That is why their vessels widen, so that more blood can flow through.
106717.m: During sport, wider vessels give the muscles a better blood supply.

107013.q: Which blood vessels are the finest in the human body?
107013.e: Capillaries, also called hair vessels, are the smallest blood vessels. They form a fine network that runs through almost all tissues.
107013.m: The capillaries are the finest blood vessels in the body.

107014.q: How thick is the wall of a capillary?
107014.e: The wall of a capillary is made of just one thin layer of endothelial cells. That is why substances can pass through it easily.
107014.m: Capillaries have a wafer-thin wall of just one layer of cells.

107015.q: What is the main job of the capillaries?
a: Exchanging substances between blood and tissue
107015.e: In the capillaries, oxygen and nutrients pass from the blood into the tissue. In return, the blood takes up carbon dioxide and waste.
107015.m: In the capillaries, blood and tissue exchange substances.

107016.q: Roughly what is the diameter of a typical capillary?
107016.e: Capillaries are only about 5 to 10 micrometres wide, which is much thinner than a hair. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre.
107016.m: A capillary is much thinner than a human hair.

107017.q: How do red blood cells move through the narrowest capillaries?
a: Not at all, they stay still
107017.e: The narrowest capillaries are hardly wider than a red blood cell. The blood cells change shape and squeeze through one at a time.
107017.m: In narrow capillaries, red blood cells line up one by one.

107018.q: Between which blood vessels do the capillaries lie?
a: Between the windpipe and the lungs
Between the stomach and the intestines
107018.e: The blood flows from the arteries through the fine capillaries into the veins and from there back to the heart.
107018.m: The capillaries connect arteries and veins.

107019.q: Which gas do the capillaries in a working muscle mainly give off?
107019.e: The blood brings oxygen to the muscle cells, which need it to make energy. In return the blood takes up carbon dioxide.
